What has not changed? The effort level and total surplus are identical across the two columns, and the manager earns exactly her outside option in both. On every measure of efficiency, the franchise contract matches the first-best.
What has inverted? The risk allocation has flipped. In the first-best with observable effort, the risk-neutral owner bore all income risk and the manager received a certain fixed wage. Under the franchise contract, the manager bears all of it.
Why is this costless here? For a risk-neutral manager the inversion is inconsequential. She is indifferent between a certain payment of \(p_{e^*}\pi_H + (1-p_{e^*})\pi_L - \alpha^*\) and the variable payment with that same expected value, because risk neutrality means she demands no premium for bearing income variance.
Why will this not survive risk aversion? For a risk-averse manager, the franchise contract imposes a real cost. She suffers a utility loss from bearing income risk and will demand a risk premium on top of her outside option, driving up the cost of the contract to the owner. Any attempt to reduce her risk exposure, by making wages less sensitive to outcomes, simultaneously weakens her incentive to exert effort, since she is no longer the full residual claimant.
This is the insurance–incentives trade-off, the irreducible tension at the heart of moral hazard theory. It does not arise under risk neutrality, because the cost of bearing risk is zero. Once risk aversion enters, the trade-off binds. That is the subject of the next section.



3.3.5 Moral Hazard with a Risk-Averse Manager

3.3.5.1 The formal problem
The owner’s strategy is to choose a target effort level \(e \in \{e_L, e_H\}\) and a pair of wages \((w_H, w_L)\) that minimises the expected cost of implementing that effort, then to compare net payoffs across the two effort levels.
The cost-minimisation problem. For a given target effort \(e\), with alternative \(e'\), the problem is
\[
\min_{(w_H, w_L)} \; p_e\, w_H + (1-p_e)\, w_L
\]
subject to
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(IR)} \quad & p_e\, v(w_H) + (1-p_e)\, v(w_L) - g(e) \geq \overline{u} \\[6pt]
\text{(IC)} \quad & p_e\, v(w_H) + (1-p_e)\, v(w_L) - g(e) \geq p_{e'}\, v(w_H) + (1-p_{e'})\, v(w_L) - g(e')
\end{aligned}
\]
Understanding the constraint set. (IR) requires that the manager’s expected utility under the contract be no less than her outside option \(\overline{u}\). Without it, she walks away. (IC) requires that, given the wages \((w_H, w_L)\), the manager prefers to exert effort \(e\) over the available deviation \(e'\). Because the owner cannot observe effort, she can neither prevent deviations by contract nor monitor them. The contract must therefore be self-enforcing: high effort must be a best response for the manager.
This is the structural departure from the first-best. There, the owner faced a single binding constraint and dictated effort. Here she faces two, and they pull in opposite directions.
Simplifying the constraint for the binary case. Collecting terms, the (IC) for implementing \(e_H\) reduces to a single inequality:
\[
\underbrace{(p_H - p_L)}_{\text{shift in the odds}} \cdot \underbrace{\bigl[v(w_H) - v(w_L)\bigr]}_{\text{utility spread the contract offers}} \;\geq\; \underbrace{g(e_H) - g(e_L)}_{\equiv\, \Delta g \;>\; 0}
\]
The left-hand side is the expected marginal benefit of effort to the manager: working harder raises the chance of the good outcome by \(p_H - p_L\), and the good outcome is worth \(v(w_H) - v(w_L)\) more to her than the bad one. The right-hand side is the marginal cost she bears personally.
Three things follow immediately.

A flat wage cannot implement \(e_H\). With \(w_H = w_L\) the left-hand side is zero and the inequality fails, since \(\Delta g > 0\).
The required spread is \(v(w_H) - v(w_L) \geq \Delta g / (p_H - p_L)\). The manager must be exposed to risk, and the ratio says how much.
The noisier the signal, meaning the smaller \(p_H - p_L\), the larger that spread must be. As \(p_H \to p_L\) it grows without bound, and high effort becomes impossible to buy.



3.3.5.2 Implementing low effort
As in the observable-effort case, begin by fixing the target effort level and then derive the minimum wage needed to implement it. Start with the low-effort case.
The optimal way to implement \(e_L\) turns out to be simple: the (IC) constraint is redundant, imposing no restriction beyond what (IR) already requires. The problem therefore reduces to the first-best cost-minimisation problem, and the solution is identical.
Targeting \(e_L\) means the owner needs a contract under which the manager weakly prefers \(e_L\) to the deviation \(e_H\), so the (IC) requires
\[
-(p_H - p_L)\bigl[v(w_H) - v(w_L)\bigr] \;\geq\; -\Delta g
\]
Since \(\Delta g > 0\), the right-hand side is strictly negative. The (IC) is therefore satisfied so long as the gain from deviating to \(e_H\) is not too large. A flat wage, which sets \(v(w_H) - v(w_L) = 0\), satisfies it strictly.
The expected cost of implementing \(e_L\) is therefore the same whether effort is observable or not. Moral hazard imposes no cost at all in this regime, which is why the entire welfare cost of the problem is concentrated in the high-effort case examined next.


3.3.5.3 Implementing high effort
The owner’s problem. The owner minimises expected wages subject to both constraints:
\[
\min_{(w_H, w_L)} \; p_H\, w_H + (1-p_H)\, w_L
\]
subject to
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(IR)} \quad & p_H\, v(w_H) + (1-p_H)\, v(w_L) - g(e_H) \geq \overline{u} \\[6pt]
\text{(IC)} \quad & (p_H - p_L)\bigl[v(w_H) - v(w_L)\bigr] \geq \Delta g
\end{aligned}
\]
Unlike the low-effort case, neither constraint can be set aside here. The results that follow establish that both bind at the optimum.
The Lagrangean and the first-order condition. The Lagrangean is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L} = &-\bigl[p_H\, w_H + (1-p_H)\, w_L\bigr] + \gamma \Bigl[p_H\, v(w_H) + (1-p_H)\, v(w_L) - g(e_H) - \overline{u}\Bigr] \\
&+ \mu \Bigl[(p_H - p_L)\bigl(v(w_H) - v(w_L)\bigr) - \Delta g\Bigr]
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\Delta g \equiv g(e_H) - g(e_L) > 0\), \(\gamma \geq 0\) is the multiplier on (IR) and \(\mu \geq 0\) the multiplier on (IC).
Differentiating with respect to each wage:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w_H} &= -p_H + \gamma\, v'(w_H)\, p_H + \mu\, v'(w_H)\,(p_H - p_L) = 0 \\[4pt]
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w_L} &= -(1-p_H) + \gamma\, v'(w_L)\,(1-p_H) - \mu\, v'(w_L)\,(p_H - p_L) = 0
\end{aligned}
\]
Dividing each by its probability and rearranging gives the pair
\[
\frac{1}{v'(w_H^{**})} = \gamma + \mu\!\left[1 - \frac{p_L}{p_H}\right],
\qquad
\frac{1}{v'(w_L^{**})} = \gamma + \mu\!\left[1 - \frac{1-p_L}{1-p_H}\right]
\]
Both have the same shape. Writing \(\ell_i \equiv \Pr(\pi_i \mid e_L) / \Pr(\pi_i \mid e_H)\) for the likelihood ratio of outcome \(i\), so that \(\ell_H = p_L/p_H\) and \(\ell_L = (1-p_L)/(1-p_H)\), each condition reads
\[
\frac{1}{v'(w_i^{**})} = \gamma + \mu\bigl[1 - \ell_i\bigr], \qquad i \in \{L, H\}.
\]
This first-order condition, due to Mirrlees (1976) and Holmström (1979), is the central equation of principal–agent theory, and it takes the same form however many outcomes there are. Every important result of the model follows from reading it carefully.
Reading the first-order condition. The left-hand side, \(1/v'(w)\), is the marginal cost of delivering one additional unit of utility to the manager at wage \(w\). Because \(v\) is strictly concave, \(v'\) is strictly decreasing, so \(1/v'(w)\) is strictly increasing in \(w\). Transferring utility to the manager is cheap when she is poorly paid, since each pound buys a lot of utility, and expensive when she is well paid.
The right-hand side has two components:

\(\gamma\) is the shadow cost of (IR): the baseline cost of attracting the manager, independent of any incentive consideration.
\(\mu\bigl[1 - \ell_i\bigr]\) is the incentive adjustment: the premium or discount applied to outcome \(\pi_i\) according to how informative that outcome is about whether the manager exerted high effort.

The likelihood ratio does all the work in what follows. Since \(p_H > p_L\), the good outcome has \(\ell_H < 1\) and attracts a premium, while the bad outcome has \(\ell_L > 1\) and attracts a discount. Pay attaches to evidence of effort, not to profit as such: here the two coincide, because with only two outcomes the profitable one is also the one that is evidence of effort.


3.3.5.4 Three implications of the first-order condition

Result 1: both constraints bind. At any solution to the cost-minimisation problem when \(e_H\) is the target effort, \(\gamma > 0\) and \(\mu > 0\).
Proof.

Suppose \(\gamma = 0\). The owner could then reduce the wage paid in the low-profit outcome slightly without violating (IC), giving a better contract that still implements \(e_H\). This contradicts optimality, so \(\gamma > 0\) and (IR) binds.
Suppose \(\mu = 0\). The owner could then reduce the manager’s risk slightly by decreasing the wage paid in the high-profit outcome and increasing the wage paid in the low-profit outcome, without violating (IC). Lower risk means the manager will participate for a lower expected wage, giving a better contract that still implements \(e_H\). This contradicts optimality, so \(\mu > 0\) and (IC) binds.



Result 2: the manager bears risk, and is paid more after the good outcome. The second-best contract satisfies \(w_H^{**} > \tilde{w} > w_L^{**}\), where \(\tilde{w}\) is the wage defined by \(1/v'(\tilde{w}) = \gamma\). In particular \(w_H^{**} > w_L^{**}\): the manager is not fully insured, and pay rises with profit.
Proof. From the first-order condition, \(1/v'(w_i^{**}) = \gamma + \mu[1 - \ell_i]\), and \(\mu > 0\) by Result 1, so the wage is strictly decreasing in the likelihood ratio \(\ell_i\). Since \(p_H > p_L\),
\[
\ell_H = \frac{p_L}{p_H} < 1 < \frac{1-p_L}{1-p_H} = \ell_L,
\]
so the good outcome carries a premium over \(\tilde{w}\) and the bad outcome a discount. Because \(v'' < 0\) under risk aversion, \(1/v'\) is strictly increasing, and the ordering of \(1/v'(w_i^{**})\) carries over to the wages themselves.
What the ordering means. The good outcome is paid more because it is evidence of high effort, not because there is more money to share in that state. In general the wage lies above \(\tilde{w}\) where \(\ell_i < 1\), so that the outcome is more likely under \(e_H\); below \(\tilde{w}\) where \(\ell_i > 1\); and at \(\tilde{w}\) wherever \(\ell_i = 1\) and the outcome says nothing about effort. With two outcomes, \(p_H > p_L\) is all that is needed for the evidence ranking and the profit ranking to coincide.


What changes with more than two outcomes
With two outcomes, “pay rises with profit” and “pay rises with evidence of effort” say the same thing, since there is only one way to order two outcomes. With a longer profit ladder they can come apart. The wage is still ordered by the likelihood ratio, but that ordering need not match the ordering of profits, and pay rises with profit only if \(\ell_i\) falls as \(\pi_i\) rises, a condition known as the monotone likelihood ratio property.
It can fail. Consider a manager who “swings for the fences” with a high-variance strategy. Very high profits may then be more likely under a risk-taking, low-effort manager than under a diligent, conservative one, so a spectacular result is evidence of gambling rather than of effort. The optimal contract then penalises extreme outcomes. This is directly relevant to executive compensation in financial services, where uncapped short-run bonuses can reward risk-taking at the expense of long-run value.


Result 3: the agency cost is strictly positive. The agency cost of moral hazard is defined as
\[
AC \;\equiv\; \underbrace{p_H\, w_H^{**} + (1-p_H)\, w_L^{**}}_{\text{second-best expected wage}} \;-\; \underbrace{v^{-1}\!\bigl(\overline{u} + g(e_H)\bigr)}_{w_{e_H}^*\;:\;\text{first-best fixed wage}}
\]
and it is strictly positive: \(AC > 0\).
Proof. Both constraints bind by Result 1, so the binding (IR) gives
\[
p_H\, v(w_H^{**}) + (1-p_H)\, v(w_L^{**}) = \overline{u} + g(e_H)
\]
Since \(\mu > 0\), the two wages differ. Applying Jensen’s inequality with the strict concavity of \(v\):
\[
v\!\bigl(p_H\, w_H^{**} + (1-p_H)\, w_L^{**}\bigr) \;>\; p_H\, v(w_H^{**}) + (1-p_H)\, v(w_L^{**}) \;=\; \overline{u} + g(e_H)
\]
Applying the strictly increasing inverse \(v^{-1}\) to both sides:
\[
p_H\, w_H^{**} + (1-p_H)\, w_L^{**} \;>\; v^{-1}\!\bigl(\overline{u} + g(e_H)\bigr) = w_{e_H}^*
\]
Hence \(AC > 0\): delivering the same expected utility through a variable wage costs strictly more than delivering it through a certain one.

The proof of Result 3 reveals the exact source of the agency cost. It is the risk premium the owner must pay to compensate the risk-averse manager for bearing the income variance that (IC) forces upon her.
The distortion can be seen directly in contract space.



Reading the diagram:

The full-insurance line. The 45° line represents equal wages in the good and bad states. In the first-best the contract lies on this line, so the manager bears no risk at all.
The participation curve. The curve \(IR_H\) is the manager’s indifference curve through \(e_H\) at utility \(\overline{u}\). It represents every contract giving her exactly her outside option when she exerts high effort. Because (IR) binds, the optimal contract must lie somewhere on this curve.
The incentive curve. (IC) requires the contract to lie on or above the curve \(IC \equiv IR_L\), the set of contracts under which the manager is just indifferent between \(e_H\) and \(e_L\). Contracts strictly above this curve induce high effort; contracts below it induce low effort.
The second-best contract. Since both constraints bind, the optimal contract sits at point \(C\), the intersection of \(IR_H\) and \(IC\). This point lies strictly off the 45° line, so the manager bears some income risk. It also lies below the first-best contract on \(IR_H\), and that gap is the agency cost.



3.3.5.5 Structural properties of the second-best contract
The optimal contract implementing \(e_H\) has four features:

Partial risk exposure: The two wages differ, since \(\mu > 0\), but by strictly less than under the franchise contract, where the spread is the full \(\pi_H - \pi_L\). The manager bears some, but not all, income risk.
Informativeness-based pay: The premium or penalty at an outcome is determined by its likelihood ratio \(\ell_i\), not by the profit level itself. The good outcome is rewarded because it is evidence of high effort, and the size of the reward is set by \(\Delta g/(p_H - p_L)\), the utility spread (IC) demands.
Strictly positive agency cost: \(AC > 0\), so the owner’s expected profit falls strictly below the first-best. This is the deadweight loss from the information asymmetry, and no contract can eliminate it however cleverly designed.
Zero rents for the manager: Both constraints bind, so she earns exactly \(\overline{u}\). The entire agency cost falls on the owner.


Why can the conflict not be resolved?
The results so far establish a structural asymmetry: moral hazard is distortionary if and only if the owner targets the higher effort level. When she targets \(e_L\), any flat wage satisfying (IR) with equality automatically satisfies (IC) strictly. The manager would bear the full incremental disutility \(\Delta g > 0\) from deviating to \(e_H\), while her expected pay would be unchanged, since a flat wage pays the same whichever outcome occurs and effort only shifts the odds between outcomes. Deviation is strictly unprofitable, so the entire welfare cost of moral hazard is concentrated in the high-effort regime.
In that regime, two requirements pull in opposite directions and cannot both be satisfied at once:

Efficient risk sharing calls for a flat wage, one that does not depend on which outcome is realised. With a risk-averse manager and a risk-neutral owner, optimal insurance means the manager bears no outcome risk.
Incentive compatibility calls for a variable wage. The manager must actually prefer \(e_H\) to \(e_L\), and since effort is costly and unobservable, the only way to make high effort attractive is to tie her pay to outcomes, rewarding good results and penalising bad ones.

A contract cannot do both. The second-best resolves the conflict by conceding partial risk exposure, and the agency cost is what that concession costs the owner.



3.3.5.6 When is high effort socially worthwhile?
High effort is implemented if and only if
\[
\underbrace{\bigl[p_H \pi_H + (1-p_H)\pi_L\bigr] - \bigl[p_H w_H^{**} + (1-p_H) w_L^{**}\bigr]}_{\text{owner's expected profit under } e_H} \;\geq\; \underbrace{\bigl[p_L \pi_H + (1-p_L)\pi_L\bigr] - w_{e_L}^*}_{\text{owner's expected profit under } e_L}
\]
Rearranging, the condition requires that the gain in expected output from \(e_H\) outweighs the additional total compensation cost:
\[
\underbrace{(p_H - p_L)(\pi_H - \pi_L)}_{\text{expected output gain}} \;\geq\; \underbrace{\bigl[p_H w_H^{**} + (1-p_H) w_L^{**}\bigr] - w_{e_L}^*}_{\text{additional compensation cost}}
\]
The right-hand side now exceeds the first-best implementation cost by the agency cost. This implies a key and often overlooked result: the owner may choose to implement low effort even where high effort would be socially efficient, if the agency cost of inducing high effort is sufficiently large.
Moral hazard therefore causes not just a distortion in the form of the contract, but a distortion in the effort level chosen. This is a second layer of efficiency loss.


3.3.5.7 Comparative statics
High effort is less likely to be implemented when:

The manager is more risk averse: She demands a larger risk premium to bear incentive risk, raising the agency cost. Formally, greater concavity in \(v\) implies a larger gap between the expected wage and its certainty equivalent.
The effort productivity gap is smaller: If \((p_H - p_L)(\pi_H - \pi_L)\) is small, the output benefit of high effort is modest and the agency cost may exceed it.
Outcome noise is greater: When profits are driven mainly by factors outside the manager’s control, they are a weak signal of effort. Formally, (IC) requires \(v(w_H) - v(w_L) \geq \Delta g / (p_H - p_L)\), so as the odds shift \(p_H - p_L\) shrinks, the required spread grows without bound. The manager is made to bear a great deal of risk, most of it rewarding or penalising luck rather than effort, for very little incentive benefit.
The manager’s outside option works differently: A higher \(\overline{u}\) raises the fixed cost of satisfying (IR) whichever effort is targeted, without affecting the agency cost directly. Since it raises the cost of implementing \(e_H\) and \(e_L\) alike, its net effect on the effort decision depends on the curvature of \(v\).

Why noise matters. The third of these comparative statics deserves particular emphasis: in noisier environments the agency cost of high effort is larger, so it may be optimal to abandon high-powered incentives entirely.
Where a manager’s compensation is determined largely by macroeconomic fluctuations, industry-wide shocks, or luck rather than her own choices, tying pay to outcomes is a blunt and costly incentive instrument. In the limit, if \(p_H = p_L\) so that profit is completely uninformative about effort, the required spread \(\Delta g/(p_H - p_L)\) is infinite: no wage pair can satisfy (IC), and the owner can only implement low effort.
This provides a formal rationale for why high-powered incentive contracts are rare in sectors where output is driven largely by aggregate factors.



3.3.6 Economic Implications and Empirical Predictions
The principal–agent model yields testable predictions about the structure of compensation contracts, insurance markets, financial regulation and agricultural organisation.

3.3.6.1 Insurance markets
This is a different insurance market from the one in the previous chapter. There, the insurer faced a hidden type, a customer who already knew her accident probability, and competition among insurers drove profits to zero. Here the insurer faces a hidden action: the risk depends on care the policyholder chooses after the policy is signed, and the insurer is a principal designing a single bilateral contract rather than a firm competing for customers in a Rothschild–Stiglitz market. Partial coverage appears in both models and does quite different work in each. Under adverse selection it separates good risks from bad; here it keeps the policyholder’s own money at stake so that she still takes care.
Within that setting, the model explains co-payments, deductibles, and coverage limits. These features are often attributed to actuarial pricing, but the model reveals a deeper rationale: they are a deliberate design response to moral hazard. By retaining some risk exposure for the insured party, the insurer maintains a financial incentive for the policyholder to take preventive action.
The cost is that policyholders are not fully insured, so the contract is second-best from a risk-sharing perspective. This is the price of information asymmetry. The optimal insurance contract balances the gain from risk reduction against the cost of weakened prevention incentives, exactly as in the principal–agent problem.
Empirical evidence on health insurance (Finkelstein et al. 2012; Einav et al. 2013) and on motor insurance (Abbring, Chiappori and Pinquet 2003) confirms that moral hazard is quantitatively significant: coverage expansions do lead to measurable increases in utilisation and risk-taking.


3.3.6.2 Financial regulation and systemic risk
When financial institutions expect government bailouts in the event of failure, they enjoy implicit downside insurance. The model predicts, and the 2007–2008 global financial crisis confirmed, that this implicit guarantee induces excessive risk-taking. The mechanism is direct: with the downside socialised and the upside private, the bank’s incentive structure resembles holding a call option on the outcome. The socially efficient level of risk-taking is not internalised.
Regulatory responses such as capital requirements, mandatory “bail-in” debt, resolution frameworks, and restrictions on proprietary trading are best understood as mechanisms to restore the institution’s exposure to loss. They move the bank back toward the incentive side of the trade-off by ensuring that equity holders and creditors bear losses before taxpayers.
The model thus provides a principled normative basis for financial regulation that goes beyond the standard market-failure justifications.


3.3.6.3 Employment contracts and organisational design
The model explains why different occupations feature very different compensation structures. Piece rates, commissions, and profit-sharing are common in sales, real estate, and law, where individual output is observable and relatively easy to attribute to a specific agent’s effort. Flat salaries are standard in assembly-line manufacturing, public administration, and academic research, where individual contribution is hard to measure, team production is prevalent, and output variance is driven by factors outside individual control.
The model predicts precisely this pattern. High-powered incentives are optimal when:

Individual output is a precise signal of individual effort, meaning low noise.
The agent is not too risk averse.
Effort has a large effect on expected output.

When these conditions fail, flat pay with monitoring is the second-best arrangement. This prediction has been tested and confirmed in the empirical literature on incentive contracting (see Prendergast 1999 for a comprehensive survey).


3.3.6.4 Agricultural contracts and development economics
Sharecropping contracts, under which a tenant farmer remits a fixed fraction \(s \in (0,1)\) of output to the landlord, create a classic moral hazard problem. The tenant captures only \((1-s)\) of her marginal product, so her private return to effort falls strictly below the social return. The result is inefficiently low effort.
Fixed-rent tenancy, as established in the risk-neutral benchmark earlier in this section, eliminates this distortion by making the tenant the full residual claimant after a fixed payment. But for a risk-averse tenant facing significant weather or price risk, fixed rent imposes undesirable income volatility. Sharecropping provides partial insurance precisely through the profit-sharing structure that weakens incentives.
The second-best contract therefore trades off insurance, the argument for sharecropping, against incentives, the argument for fixed rent, and the optimal sharing rate \(s^*\) is an interior solution. This framework, due to Stiglitz (1974) and Cheung (1969), shaped an entire literature on agricultural organisation in developing economies, and its predictions about the prevalence of sharecropping against fixed-rent tenancy as a function of risk and monitoring costs have been extensively examined (Otsuka, Chuma, and Hayami 1992).
The same framework therefore runs from executive pay to crop-sharing agreements, and from insurance markets to prudential banking regulation. Its usefulness lies less in its generality than in the fact that its comparative statics are sharp enough to be taken to data.



3.3.7 Worked Example: Observable and Unobservable Effort
This example puts a number on the cost of moral hazard.

Setup
A risk-neutral owner hires a risk-averse manager, who chooses between two effort levels:

Shirk (\(e = S\)): zero effort cost, \(c_S = 0\).
Work hard (\(e = H\)): effort disutility of \(c_H = 10\) in money units.

Revenue outcomes depend on effort:




Revenue \(= R\)
Revenue \(= 0\)




Hard effort (\(e = H\))
probability \(0.8\)
probability \(0.2\)


Shirk (\(e = S\))
probability \(0.3\)
probability \(0.7\)



Preferences:

Manager (risk averse): utility \(= \sqrt{w} - c_j\) when paid wage \(w\) and exerting effort \(e_j\).
Owner (risk neutral): maximises expected profit \(=\) expected revenue \(-\) expected wage.

Outside option: the manager can take an outside job paying \(w = 400\) with effort cost \(5\), giving utility \(\sqrt{400} - 5 = 15\). She accepts the owner’s contract if it gives her at least \(15\). If indifferent, she stays.

Two numbers carry this example: the revenue threshold at which the owner chooses to induce hard work when she can observe effort, and the same threshold when she cannot. The gap between them is the cost of moral hazard.

3.3.7.1 Observable effort: inducing shirking
When the owner observes both effort and the revenue realisation, she can write a contract \(w(e, \text{revenue})\) that conditions wages on effort directly. Two considerations pin down the contract:

Participation (IR): The manager must prefer the contract to her outside option, so \(\sqrt{w} - 0 \geq 15\), giving \(w \geq 225\).
Cost minimisation: The owner pays no more than she must, so \(w = 225\).

Since effort is observable, the owner can simply specify shirking in the contract. She offers a flat wage of \(225\) regardless of the revenue outcome. A flat wage is efficient here because the risk-neutral owner should absorb all income risk, and with effort contractible there is no incentive reason to expose the manager to any of it.
Owner’s expected profit: \(0.3R - 225\).


3.3.7.2 Observable effort: inducing hard work
Two conditions apply:

Participation (IR): \(\sqrt{w_H} - 10 \geq 15\), so \(\sqrt{w_H} \geq 25\) and \(w_H \geq 625\).
Cost minimisation: set \(w_H = 625\).

Since effort is directly observable, there is no incentive problem. The owner can verify that the manager worked hard and pay \(625\) accordingly, while paying a sufficiently low wage if the manager shirks, which makes shirking unattractive.
With \(w_H = 625\), the manager’s payoff from working hard is \(\sqrt{625} - 10 = 25 - 10 = 15\), exactly her outside option.
Note what the contract does not do: the wage does not depend on the revenue realisation. The manager receives full insurance and bears no income risk.
Owner’s expected profit: \(0.8R - 625\).


3.3.7.3 Observable effort: the owner’s choice
The owner prefers hard work when
\[
0.8R - 625 \;\geq\; 0.3R - 225
\]
\[
0.5R \;\geq\; 400 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad R \;\geq\; 800
\]
Intuition. Inducing hard work raises the probability of the high revenue outcome from \(0.3\) to \(0.8\), a gain of \(0.5R\) in expected revenue, but costs an extra \(625 - 225 = 400\) in wages. It is worthwhile only when the revenue gain exceeds the wage premium.


3.3.7.4 Hidden effort: setting up the constraints
The contract can now condition only on the revenue realisation: \(w_R\) if revenue is \(R\), and \(w_0\) if revenue is \(0\).
Inducing shirking is unchanged. A flat wage \(w_R = w_0 = 225\) still works. Under a flat wage the manager has no financial reason to exert costly effort whether or not she is observed, so the optimal shirking contract is identical to the observable case, and the owner’s expected profit is again \(0.3R - 225\).
Inducing hard work now requires two constraints. The incentive compatibility constraint requires that hard work be at least as attractive as shirking:
\[
\underbrace{0.8\sqrt{w_R} + 0.2\sqrt{w_0} - 10}_{\text{utility from hard work}} \;\geq\; \underbrace{0.3\sqrt{w_R} + 0.7\sqrt{w_0}}_{\text{utility from shirking}}
\]
Rearranging gives
\[
0.5\sqrt{w_R} - 0.5\sqrt{w_0} \;\geq\; 10 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \sqrt{w_R} - \sqrt{w_0} \;\geq\; 20 \qquad \text{(IC)}
\]
The participation constraint requires that expected utility from working hard be at least the outside option:
\[
0.8\sqrt{w_R} + 0.2\sqrt{w_0} - 10 \;\geq\; 15 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad 4\sqrt{w_R} + \sqrt{w_0} \;\geq\; 125 \qquad \text{(IR)}
\]
(multiplying through by \(5\)).
Intuition. (IC) requires the wage spread to be large enough that the extra probability of a high revenue outcome under hard effort, \(0.8 - 0.3 = 0.5\), compensates the manager for the effort cost of \(10\). Pay must be sensitive to outcomes, which is precisely what the observable-effort contract avoided.


3.3.7.5 Hidden effort: the optimal contract
The owner solves
\[
\max_{w_R,\, w_0} \;\; 0.8R - 0.8w_R - 0.2w_0 \qquad \text{subject to (IC) and (IR)}
\]
Step 1: (IR) binds. Suppose it did not, so the manager earns a strict surplus above \(15\). The owner could then lower \(w_0\) slightly. This reduces the wage bill and relaxes (IC), since a lower \(w_0\) widens the spread \(\sqrt{w_R} - \sqrt{w_0}\). Both constraints would still hold at a lower cost, contradicting optimality. Hence
\[
4\sqrt{w_R} + \sqrt{w_0} = 125 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \sqrt{w_0} = 125 - 4\sqrt{w_R}
\]
Step 2: substitute into (IC).
\[
\sqrt{w_R} - \bigl(125 - 4\sqrt{w_R}\bigr) \geq 20 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad 5\sqrt{w_R} \geq 145 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \sqrt{w_R} \geq 29
\]
Step 3: solve the reduced problem. Writing \(x = \sqrt{w_R}\), so that \(w_R = x^2\) and \(w_0 = (125 - 4x)^2\), the Lagrangean is
\[
\mathcal{L} = 0.8R - 0.8x^2 - 0.2(125 - 4x)^2 + \lambda(x - 29)
\]
Differentiating:
\[
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x} = -1.6x + 1.6(125 - 4x) + \lambda = -8x + 200 + \lambda = 0 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \lambda = 8x - 200
\]
At the optimum either (IC) is slack, with \(\lambda = 0\) and \(x > 29\), or it binds, with \(\lambda > 0\) and \(x = 29\).
Setting \(\lambda = 0\) gives \(x = 25\), which is below \(29\) and violates (IC). The unconstrained optimum is therefore infeasible, so (IC) binds at \(x = 29\), giving \(\lambda = 8(29) - 200 = 32 > 0\). ✓
From the binding (IR), \(\sqrt{w_0} = 125 - 4(29) = 9\). Therefore
\[
w_R = 841, \qquad w_0 = 81
\]
Interpretation. The manager earns \(841\) if the project succeeds and only \(81\) if it fails. She bears substantial income risk, a direct consequence of effort being unverifiable, and being risk averse she dislikes that exposure. The owner must compensate her for it through higher expected wages.

The cost of moral hazard, in numbers
Hidden effort imposes two distinct costs in this example.

A higher wage bill. The owner pays \(689\) in expectation instead of \(625\), an extra \(64\). This is the risk premium the risk-averse manager demands for accepting an unequal wage contract, and it is the agency cost in this example.
A distorted effort choice. For \(R\) between \(800\) and \(928\), the owner would induce hard work if she could observe effort, but settles for shirking when she cannot. Across that range, socially valuable effort goes unprovided because the information asymmetry makes it too costly to incentivise.

The second cost is the more striking. Moral hazard distorts not only the form of the contract, through the risk the manager is forced to bear, but the level of effort the owner chooses to buy.




3.3.8 Moral Hazard with Two Manager Types
Everything so far has assumed the owner knows exactly who she is hiring. She cannot see what the manager does, but she knows what the manager is: her disutility of effort, her risk preferences and her outside option are all common knowledge. Only the action is hidden.
In practice that is a strong assumption. Some managers find hard work genuinely easier than others — through stamina, experience, better organisation, or simply a lower opportunity cost of their time — and a prospective employer rarely knows which sort is sitting across the table. This section extends the model so that the cost of effort is itself private information. The owner now faces two layers of asymmetry at once: a hidden type before contracting, and a hidden action afterwards.
This brings the chapter full circle. The screening problem we opened with was pure adverse selection; the principal–agent problem of this section was, until now, pure moral hazard. Here they operate simultaneously, and the interaction produces a result that neither model delivers on its own.

3.3.8.1 Setup
The environment is exactly as before — two outcomes \(\pi_H > \pi_L\), two effort levels, a risk-neutral owner and a risk-averse manager with utility \(v(w) - g(e)\) — with one change.
Normalise \(g_\theta(e_L) = 0\) and write \(g_\theta \equiv g_\theta(e_H)\) for the incremental disutility of high effort. The manager is one of two types:

Type \(A\) (the low-cost type) with \(g_A\), drawn with probability \(\beta\);
Type \(B\) (the high-cost type) with \(g_B > g_A\), drawn with probability \(1 - \beta\).

Write \(\Delta g \equiv g_B - g_A > 0\). The two types are identical in every other respect: same \(v(\cdot)\), same outside option \(\overline{u}\), same technology \((p_H, p_L)\). Only the price of effort differs.
Timing. Nature draws \(\theta \in \{A, B\}\); the manager privately observes it; the owner posts a menu of contracts; the manager selects one; she then chooses effort, which the owner cannot observe; the outcome realises and wages are paid.
By the revelation principle (introduced in the screening section of this chapter) it is enough to consider menus with one contract per type, \(\{C^A, C^B\}\), under which each type truthfully selects the contract meant for her.


3.3.8.2 Working in utility space
The algebra is far cleaner if the owner is treated as choosing utilities rather than wages. Let
\[
u_H = v(w_H), \qquad u_L = v(w_L), \qquad h \equiv v^{-1}
\]
so that \(h\) is increasing and convex (the inverse of an increasing concave function). The wage needed to deliver utility \(u\) is \(h(u)\). For a contract \(C = (u_H, u_L)\) define
\[
U_e(C) = p_e u_H + (1-p_e)u_L, \qquad \Delta(C) = u_H - u_L, \qquad K_e(C) = p_e h(u_H) + (1-p_e)h(u_L)
\]
so \(U_e\) is expected utility of money under effort \(e\), \(\Delta\) is the spread, and \(K_e\) is the owner’s expected wage bill. A useful identity follows directly:
\[
U_L(C) = U_H(C) - (p_H - p_L)\,\Delta(C)
\]
Because \(h\) is convex, widening the spread at a fixed \(U_H\) is a mean-preserving spread in utility and therefore strictly raises \(K_H\). The owner wants the smallest spread she can get away with, exactly as in the one-type model.


3.3.8.3 The four families of constraints
Effort incentive compatibility. To induce \(e_H\) from type \(\theta\) on contract \(C\),
\[
(p_H - p_L)\,\Delta(C) \;\geq\; g_\theta \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \Delta(C) \;\geq\; \delta_\theta \equiv \frac{g_\theta}{p_H - p_L}
\]
Since \(g_A < g_B\), we have \(\delta_A < \delta_B\): the low-cost type needs a smaller spread.
Participation. \(U_H(C^\theta) - g_\theta \geq \overline{u}\) for each type.
Type incentive compatibility. Each type must prefer its own contract. The subtlety is that a deviating manager, having taken the other type’s contract, then chooses whatever effort suits her on it. Two deviations must be checked, and they are not symmetric.

Who can mimic whom, and how

Type \(A\) taking \(C^B\) works hard. \(C^B\) must have spread at least \(\delta_B > \delta_A\), so it more than satisfies \(A\)’s own effort constraint. \(A\) gets \(U_H(C^B) - g_A\) — the same gross package \(B\) receives, but at a lower effort cost.
Type \(B\) taking \(C^A\) shirks. \(C^A\) needs a spread of only \(\delta_A < \delta_B\), which is too flat to make high effort worthwhile for \(B\). So \(B\) pockets the pay and shirks, getting \(U_L(C^A)\).

The low-cost type mimics to capture a rent; the high-cost type mimics to capture a quiet life. Both deviations constrain the menu, and the second is the one that bites.

Formally, if the owner wants both types to work hard:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(T-A)} \quad & U_H(C^A) - g_A \;\geq\; U_H(C^B) - g_A \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; U_H(C^A) \geq U_H(C^B) \\[4pt]
\text{(T-B)} \quad & U_H(C^B) - g_B \;\geq\; U_L(C^A) \;=\; U_H(C^A) - (p_H - p_L)\Delta(C^A)
\end{aligned}
\]


3.3.8.4 Result 1: the menu collapses

Proposition 3. If the owner wants both types to exert high effort, the optimal menu consists of a single contract, the one that would be offered to the high-cost type alone:
\[
U_H = \overline{u} + g_B, \qquad \Delta = \delta_B
\]
Both types accept it, both work hard, the high-cost type earns exactly her outside option, and the low-cost type earns an informational rent of exactly \(\Delta g = g_B - g_A\).
Proof. First, (IR-B) binds. Raising \(U_H(C^B)\) above \(\overline{u} + g_B\) costs the owner strictly more and relaxes nothing: it appears in (T-B) only through the combination below, which is unaffected by it.
Given \(U_H(C^B) = \overline{u} + g_B\), constraint (T-A) requires \(U_H(C^A) \geq \overline{u} + g_B\). Substituting both into (T-B) and rearranging,
\[
(p_H - p_L)\,\Delta(C^A) \;\geq\; U_H(C^A) - U_H(C^B) + g_B \;\geq\; g_B
\]
so \(\Delta(C^A) \geq \delta_B\). The owner’s cost is strictly increasing in both \(U_H(C^A)\) and \(\Delta(C^A)\), so both sit at their lower bounds: \(U_H(C^A) = \overline{u} + g_B\) and \(\Delta(C^A) = \delta_B\). But those are precisely the terms of \(C^B\), so \(C^A = C^B\). ∎

This is worth pausing on, because it is the opposite of what the screening section of this chapter led us to expect. There, the monopolist separated two consumer types by degrading the low-type product. Here the owner would like to give the low-cost manager a flatter, cheaper contract — but any contract flat enough to suit type \(A\) is a standing invitation for type \(B\) to take it and shirk. Closing that door requires widening \(A\)’s spread all the way to \(\delta_B\), at which point \(A\)’s contract is indistinguishable from \(B\)’s.

Why screening fails here
Separation requires an instrument that the two types rank differently. Under monopolistic screening that instrument was quality, and single crossing guaranteed the ranking. Here the only instrument is the wage spread — and both types dislike spread for exactly the same reason, since they share the utility function \(v\). The spread does not sort the types; it only determines who finds effort worth exerting.
So the owner cannot screen on contract terms at a given effort level. The only thing that separates these two managers is the effort they are asked to supply.

The rent follows immediately. On the pooled contract type \(A\) obtains
\[
U_H - g_A \;=\; \overline{u} + g_B - g_A \;=\; \overline{u} + \Delta g
\]
The low-cost manager is paid as though effort were as painful for her as it is for her high-cost counterpart, and keeps the difference. This is the familiar informational rent of screening models, arriving here through an entirely different route.


3.3.8.5 Result 2: separation happens through effort, not through contracts
If the owner will not pay the rent, her alternative is to stop buying effort from the high-cost type. Suppose she targets \(e_H\) from \(A\) and \(e_L\) from \(B\). Then:

\(B\)’s contract is flat at \(h(\overline{u})\), since implementing low effort imposes no incentive constraint and the cheapest way to deliver \(\overline{u}\) is full insurance.
\(A\)’s contract is her own one-type second-best: \(U_H(C^A) = \overline{u} + g_A\) with \(\Delta(C^A) = \delta_A\).

Both type constraints now hold. Type \(A\) considering \(B\)’s flat contract would shirk on it and receive \(\overline{u}\), exactly what her own contract delivers. Type \(B\) considering \(A\)’s contract would also shirk, receiving
\[
U_L(C^A) = U_H(C^A) - (p_H - p_L)\delta_A = \overline{u} + g_A - g_A = \overline{u}
\]
again exactly her own payoff. Both constraints hold with equality, so the menu is incentive compatible under the usual tie-breaking convention, and neither type earns a rent.
A third possibility is to ask neither type for effort, paying everyone the flat wage \(h(\overline{u})\).

Why the owner never asks the high-cost type alone to work
Buying effort from \(B\) costs strictly more than buying it from \(A\): \(B\) needs both a higher expected utility (\(\overline{u} + g_B\) against \(\overline{u} + g_A\)) and a wider spread (\(\delta_B\) against \(\delta_A\)), while the output gain \((p_H - p_L)(\pi_H - \pi_L)\) is the same for both. So whenever \(B\)’s effort is worth buying, \(A\)’s certainly is. Only three regimes survive.



3.3.8.6 The three regimes
Write \(S_e = p_e \pi_H + (1-p_e)\pi_L\) for expected gross profit under effort \(e\), and \(K(U, \delta)\) for the expected wage cost of a high-effort contract with expected utility \(U\) and spread \(\delta\).









Regime
Who works hard
Expected profit
Rent to type \(A\)




1. Pool on high effort
Both
\(S_H - K(\overline{u}+g_B,\ \delta_B)\)
\(\Delta g\)


2. Separate by effort
Only \(A\)
\(\beta\bigl[S_H - K(\overline{u}+g_A,\ \delta_A)\bigr] + (1-\beta)\bigl[S_L - h(\overline{u})\bigr]\)
\(0\)


3. Pool on low effort
Neither
\(S_L - h(\overline{u})\)
\(0\)



Comparing regimes 2 and 3 gives a condition identical to the one-type model, applied to type \(A\):
\[
\underbrace{S_H - S_L}_{\text{output gain}} \;\geq\; \underbrace{K(\overline{u}+g_A,\ \delta_A) - h(\overline{u})}_{\text{cost of motivating } A}
\]
Comparing regimes 1 and 2 gives the condition that is new to the two-type model:
\[
\underbrace{(1-\beta)\bigl(S_H - S_L\bigr)}_{\text{output gained from } B\text{'s effort}} \;\geq\; \underbrace{K(\overline{u}+g_B, \delta_B) - \beta K(\overline{u}+g_A, \delta_A) - (1-\beta)h(\overline{u})}_{\text{extra wage bill, including the rent paid to every } A}
\]
The right-hand side is the crux. To buy effort from the \((1-\beta)\) high-cost managers, the owner must put everyone on the expensive contract — including the \(\beta\) low-cost managers who would have worked hard for less. She pays for \(B\)’s effort twice: once in \(B\)’s own higher wage, and again in the rent conceded to every \(A\).


3.3.8.7 Worked example

Take the worked example from the previous section and add a second type. As before \(v(w) = \sqrt{w}\), \(p_H = 0.8\), \(p_L = 0.3\), \(\overline{u} = 15\), \(\pi_H = R\), \(\pi_L = 0\).
The manager is now equally likely (\(\beta = 0.5\)) to be

type \(A\) with \(g_A = 10\) — the manager of the previous section;
type \(B\) with \(g_B = 15\).

Find the optimal menu and the owner’s choice of regime as a function of \(R\).


With \(v(w) = \sqrt{w}\) we have \(h(u) = u^2\), and \(p_H - p_L = 0.5\), so the minimum spreads are
\[
\delta_A = \frac{10}{0.5} = 20, \qquad \delta_B = \frac{15}{0.5} = 30
\]
Regime 1 — pool on high effort. By Proposition 3 the single contract has \(U_H = 15 + 15 = 30\) and \(\Delta = 30\), so
\[
u_H = 30 + 0.2(30) = 36, \qquad u_L = 30 - 0.8(30) = 6
\]
\[
w_H = 36^2 = 1296, \qquad w_L = 6^2 = 36, \qquad \mathbb{E}[w] = 0.8(1296) + 0.2(36) = 1044
\]
Check the types. Type \(B\): utility \(30 - 15 = 15 = \overline{u}\), and her effort constraint \(0.5(30) = 15 \geq 15\) binds exactly. Type \(A\): utility \(30 - 10 = 20\), a rent of \(5 = \Delta g\), and her effort constraint \(15 \geq 10\) is slack, so she works hard willingly.
Expected profit: \(0.8R - 1044\).
Regime 2 — separate by effort. Type \(A\) receives her own second-best contract, \(U_H = 15 + 10 = 25\) with \(\Delta = 20\):
\[
u_H = 29,\quad u_L = 9 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad w_H = 841,\ w_L = 81,\ \mathbb{E}[w] = 689
\]
— precisely the contract derived in the one-type example. Type \(B\) receives the flat wage \(15^2 = 225\) and shirks. Checking (T-B): type \(B\) taking \(A\)’s contract and shirking earns \(0.3(29) + 0.7(9) = 15\), exactly her own payoff, so she does not deviate.
Expected profit: \(0.5\,[0.8R - 689] + 0.5\,[0.3R - 225] = 0.55R - 457\).
Regime 3 — pool on low effort. Flat wage \(225\), nobody works hard. Expected profit: \(0.3R - 225\).
The owner’s choice.



Comparison
Condition
Threshold




Regime 2 against 3
\(0.55R - 457 \geq 0.3R - 225\)
\(R \geq 928\)


Regime 1 against 2
\(0.8R - 1044 \geq 0.55R - 457\)
\(R \geq 2348\)



So the owner pools on low effort for \(R < 928\); buys effort from the low-cost type only for \(928 \leq R < 2348\); and puts everyone on the high-powered contract for \(R \geq 2348\).
The first threshold, \(928\), is exactly the one from the one-type example — unsurprisingly, since type \(A\) is that manager. The second threshold is new, and it is high: at \(R = 2348\) the owner is paying an extra \(1044 - 689 = 355\) per low-cost manager purely to bring the high-cost ones along.



3.3.8.8 What the second type changes

Four lessons from the two-type model

Screening on contract terms is impossible. Both types dislike wage risk identically, so the spread cannot sort them. The owner’s only separating instrument is the effort she asks for, which is why the optimal “both work hard” menu is a single contract.
The low-cost type earns a rent of exactly \(\Delta g\). She is paid as if effort cost her \(g_B\) and pockets the difference. As in the screening model, the rent accrues to the type whose incentive constraint binds — here the one who finds it cheapest to imitate.
The distortion falls on the high-cost type, and it is a distortion of effort. Over the intermediate range of \(R\) she is deliberately left on a flat wage and allowed to shirk, even though her effort would be socially valuable. This is the two-type analogue of “distortion at the bottom”: the quantity being distorted is effort rather than quality.
Hidden types make high-powered incentives rarer. The threshold for putting everyone on an incentive contract rises from \(928\) to \(2348\), because the owner must pay the rent to every low-cost manager in order to motivate the high-cost ones. Uncertainty about who the agent is, on top of uncertainty about what she does, pushes the firm further towards flat pay.


The last point connects back to the empirical patterns discussed earlier. Flat salaries are common not only where output is a noisy signal of effort, but also where the workforce is heterogeneous in ways the employer cannot observe — because any incentive scheme strong enough to motivate the marginal employee overpays everyone who was already willing to work.

Question 1. In the two-type model with hidden effort costs, why does the optimal menu collapse to a single contract when the owner wants both types to work hard?

Because the two types have the same outside option, so they must receive the same contract.
Because the revelation principle rules out menus with more than one item.
Because any contract flat enough to suit the low-cost type would be taken by the high-cost type, who would then shirk.
Because the low-cost type’s participation constraint binds, leaving no room to differentiate.


Try again. A common outside option does not force a common contract — the types could in principle be offered different spreads. What rules that out is the high-cost type’s incentive to take the flatter contract and shirk on it.


Try again. The revelation principle does the opposite: it says it is enough to consider menus with one contract per type. The collapse to a single contract is a result of the constraints, not of the principle.


Well done. The low-cost type only needs spread \(\delta_A\), but a contract with that spread is too flat to make high effort worthwhile for the high-cost type, who would take it and shirk. Deterring that requires widening the low-cost contract’s spread to \(\delta_B\), at which point the two contracts coincide.


Try again. It is the high-cost type whose participation constraint binds. The low-cost type earns a strictly positive rent of \(\Delta g\), so her participation constraint is slack.



Question 2. In the worked example, the owner’s threshold for putting everyone on a high-powered contract is \(R \geq 2348\), well above the one-type threshold of \(R \geq 928\). What accounts for the gap?

The high-cost type is more risk averse, so she demands a larger risk premium.
To motivate the high-cost managers the owner must put the low-cost managers on the same expensive contract, paying each of them a rent of \(\Delta g\).
The probability of the good outcome falls when the workforce is heterogeneous.
The high-cost type’s participation constraint is slack, so she must be paid above her outside option.


Try again. Both types share the same utility function \(v(w) = \sqrt{w}\) and so the same attitude to risk. They differ only in the disutility of effort, \(g_\theta\).


Well done. Since the menu collapses, the only way to buy effort from the high-cost types is to place everyone on the contract tailored to them. Each low-cost manager then costs \(1044\) instead of \(689\) — an extra \(355\) — and that overpayment is the rent \(\Delta g\) expressed in wages.


Try again. The technology \((p_H, p_L)\) is identical for both types. What changes with heterogeneity is the cost of inducing effort, not the probability with which effort delivers the good outcome.


Try again. The high-cost type’s participation constraint binds: she earns exactly \(\overline{u} = 15\). It is the low-cost type who is paid above her outside option.





Quick Check-In
Test your understanding of the moral hazard material.

Question 1. When the owner targets low effort \(e_L\), the (IC) constraint imposes no restriction beyond the (IR). Why?

Because low effort is always the socially efficient effort level.
Because under a flat wage the manager’s expected pay is unaffected by effort, while high effort carries strictly positive disutility.
Because the owner can verify low effort at zero cost.
Because the participation constraint fails under low effort.


Try again. Whether \(e_L\) or \(e_H\) is efficient depends on the output gain from effort. The redundancy of (IC) here is a separate, purely incentive-based point.


Well done. With a constant wage the manager is paid the same whichever outcome occurs, so shifting the odds from \(p_L\) to \(p_H\) leaves her expected pay untouched: she gains nothing financially from deviating to \(e_H\) but bears \(g(e_H) - g(e_L) > 0\). She strictly prefers to shirk, and (IC) holds with slack. This is why the entire welfare cost of moral hazard is concentrated in the high-effort regime.


Try again. Effort remains unobservable throughout. Nothing about the monitoring technology changes when the target effort changes.


Try again. (IR) binds at \(w = v^{-1}(\bar{u} + g(e_L))\), exactly as in the first-best. It is satisfied, not violated.



Question 2. Under bilateral risk neutrality the franchise, or `sell the firm’, contract \(w(\pi) = \pi - \alpha^*\) achieves the first-best. What is the mechanism?

The fixed fee \(\alpha^*\) allows the owner to monitor effort indirectly.
The manager becomes the full residual claimant, so her private problem coincides with the social planner’s.
Risk is eliminated from the relationship entirely.
The manager earns a strictly positive rent, which motivates effort.


Try again. No monitoring occurs. The contract works by changing who holds the residual claim, not by revealing effort.


Well done. Since \(\alpha\) does not vary with \(e\), the manager’s objective reduces to \(\max_e \; p_e \pi_H + (1-p_e)\pi_L - g(e)\), which is exactly the surplus-maximisation problem. She internalises the full marginal return to effort, so (IC) is satisfied trivially at \(e^*\) and no wedge remains.


Try again. Risk is not eliminated, it is reallocated: the manager now bears all of it. That is costless only because she is risk neutral, which is precisely why the result does not survive risk aversion.


Try again. (IR) binds, so she earns exactly \(\bar{u}\). Effort is motivated by marginal incentives, not by the level of her payoff.



Question 3. In the second-best contract with a risk-averse manager, what determines the wage attached to each outcome?

The level of profit, since a better outcome means more to share.
The likelihood ratio \(\ell_i = \Pr(\pi_i \mid e_L) / \Pr(\pi_i \mid e_H)\).
The manager’s degree of risk aversion alone.
The variance of profits under high effort.


Try again. Pay tracks profit only indirectly. Two outcomes with very different profit levels attract the same wage if they are equally informative about effort.


Well done. The first-order condition gives \(1/v'(w_i^{**}) = \gamma + \mu[1 - \ell_i]\). Since \(\mu > 0\), the wage is strictly decreasing in the likelihood ratio: outcomes that are evidence of high effort are rewarded, outcomes that are evidence of shirking are penalised. Here \(\ell_H = p_L/p_H < 1 < (1-p_L)/(1-p_H) = \ell_L\), so the good outcome is the one that is paid more. Pay attaches to evidence, and with two outcomes the evidence happens to run the same way as profit.


Try again. Risk aversion shapes how costly the required variation is, through the curvature of \(v\), but the pattern of rewards across outcomes is set by the likelihood ratio.


Try again. Outcome noise matters for whether high effort is worth implementing at all, but it does not determine which individual outcomes are rewarded.



Question 4. The agency cost of moral hazard, \(AC > 0\), is strictly positive. What is its source?

The cost of monitoring the manager’s effort.
The rents the manager extracts from her private information.
The risk premium the owner must pay to compensate the manager for the income variance that (IC) forces upon her.
The additional disutility of effort \(g(e_H) - g(e_L)\).


Try again. No monitoring takes place in the model. The cost arises even though the owner spends nothing on observation.


Try again. Both constraints bind, so she earns exactly \(\bar{u}\) and zero rents. The entire agency cost falls on the owner. This is a sharp contrast with the screening model of Section 2, where the high type does capture a rent.


Well done. Because \(\mu > 0\), the optimal schedule is non-constant. Jensen’s inequality then implies that delivering \(\bar{u} + g(e_H)\) through a variable wage costs strictly more in expectation than the certain wage \(v^{-1}(\bar{u} + g(e_H))\). The gap is the risk premium, and no contract design can eliminate it.


Try again. That cost is present in the first-best too, and is already compensated there. The agency cost is measured net of it, as the gap between the second-best and first-best wage bills.



Question 5. In which environment are high-powered incentive contracts least likely to be optimal?

Where effort has a large effect on the distribution of output.
Where individual output is a precise signal of individual effort.
Where output is driven largely by aggregate shocks and luck.
Where the manager is close to risk neutral.


Try again. A large productivity gap makes high effort more worth buying, so high-powered incentives become more attractive.


Try again. This is the classic case for piece rates and commissions, as seen in sales and real estate.


Well done. When \(p_H - p_L\) is small, (IC) requires a utility spread of at least \(\Delta g/(p_H - p_L)\), so the wage gap must be very large, and most of it rewards or penalises luck. The manager bears substantial risk for little incentive gain, so the agency cost is high and flat pay with monitoring becomes the second-best arrangement. This explains flat salaries in public administration and academic research.


Try again. A near-risk-neutral agent demands almost no risk premium, so the agency cost approaches zero and the franchise-style contract is close to optimal.

3.4 Wrap-Up

3.4.1 Three Responses to Asymmetric Information
This chapter has examined three settings in which one party knows something the other does not. The friction is the same in each case. What differs is the instrument available to resolve it, and how much of the resulting loss each party bears.










Screening
Cheap talk
Moral hazard




What is hidden
Type (valuation)
State of the world
Action (effort)


When
Before contracting
No contract at all
After contracting


Instrument
Menu of contracts
Words alone
Outcome-contingent pay


What binds
(IR-L), (IC-H)
Sender’s indifference at each boundary
(IR) and (IC), when high effort is targeted


Who bears the loss
Monopolist: rent plus degradation cost; low type indifferent
Both parties, through coarseness
Owner, through the risk premium




3.4.1.1 What is hidden, and when?
The three problems are distinguished by the timing of the informational gap, not by its size.
Under screening the gap exists before anyone signs anything. The consumer already knows her valuation, and the monopolist’s task is to design a menu that makes her act on it. Cheap talk sits outside contracting altogether: the sender observes a state, and the only question is what she can credibly say about it. Under moral hazard there is nothing to reveal at the point of contracting, because the manager has not yet decided how hard to work; the contract must make the desired action attractive once it is in force.
That timing difference is what selects the instrument. A menu works on information the agent already holds. Where no menu and no scheme is available, all that remains is a message. An incentive scheme works on a choice the agent has yet to make.


3.4.1.2 Does private information pay?
It is tempting to assume the informed party always profits from knowing more. She does not.
Under screening she does. The high type captures a rent of \((\theta_H - \theta_L)q_B\), and she captures it precisely because (IC-H) binds: the monopolist must concede a discount to stop her taking the cheaper contract. Degrading the low-type product is the firm’s attempt to shrink that concession.
Under cheap talk she is actively worse off for the misalignment. Ex ante the sender’s expected payoff is the receiver’s, shifted down by \(b^{2}\): her own bias is what makes her unable to communicate precisely, and she bears the cost of that inability.
Under moral hazard with a known manager she captures nothing. Both constraints bind, so the manager earns exactly her outside option \(\overline{u}\), and the entire agency cost falls on the owner. Her private information destroys surplus without transferring any of it to her. Only when her type is also hidden, as in the two-type extension, does she capture a rent — and then only the low-cost type does, and only \(\Delta g\) of it. Having private information is not the same as being able to profit from it.


3.4.1.3 What is each party assumed to be able to commit to?
Commitment is not a trait that principals possess in greater or lesser degree. It is an assumption about the setting being modelled, and in each of the three models it does a great deal of work.

Screening. The monopolist posts the menu first and is bound by it. That is a fair description of a published price list or product range, which cannot be rewritten for a particular customer once she has revealed her hand by choosing. Remove the assumption and the firm would want to renegotiate with a consumer who has just identified herself as a high type, which she anticipates; the problem becomes a dynamic one, and the menu derived above is no longer optimal.
Cheap talk. Neither party commits to anything. The sender cannot bind herself to report truthfully, and the receiver cannot bind herself to act on the report in any particular way. Both assumptions matter, and relaxing either one gives a different and well-studied model:

If the sender could commit in advance, before learning the state, to how her message would depend on it, the problem becomes one of Bayesian persuasion (Kamenica and Gentzkow, 2011). She would then be choosing an information structure rather than a message, and would generally do strictly better than cheap talk allows.
If the receiver could commit to how she will act on each report, the problem becomes one of optimal delegation (Holmström, 1984; Dessein, 2002). Handing the decision to the sender outright is one such commitment, and often a better one than asking for a report.

Moral hazard. The owner commits to the wage schedule, but can write it only on what a court could check, which here is realised profit. Effort is excluded not because the owner lacks commitment power but because it is unobservable, and it is that restriction on the contracting space that puts the first-best out of reach.

Each model leaves a specific quantity on the table: the rent \((\theta_H - \theta_L)q_B\) conceded to the high type and the quality withheld from the low type in the screening problem; the risk premium paid to a manager forced to bear income risk under moral hazard; the within-cell variance the receiver cannot resolve under cheap talk. Identifying which constraint binds, and what relaxing it would be worth, is what allows the framework to be applied well beyond the three settings examined here: auctions, income taxation, regulation, financial supervision, and the design of institutions generally.



3.4.2 Key Takeaways

3.4.2.1 Monopolistic screening
When a monopolist cannot observe how much each consumer values quality, it designs a menu of price–quality pairs that induces consumers to reveal their type through choice. Two constraints bind at the optimum: the low type’s participation constraint and the high type’s incentive compatibility constraint. Everything else follows from those two.
The solution delivers four robust predictions: full rent extraction from the lowest type, informational rents for every type above, no distortion at the top, and downward distortion of every allocation below it. The damaged good is the instrument that buys back rent at the top by distorting quality at the bottom, and the firm will pay real resources to produce it even though degradation generates no consumer value.
Screening is only a middle-ground strategy in the type mix. Pooling at a low price sweeps the whole market when high types are rare; excluding low types altogether wins when high types are numerous. The damaged good is optimal only in the band between.


3.4.2.2 Cheap talk
Cheap talk is communication that is costless, unverifiable and non-binding. Credibility cannot come from a signalling cost, as it does in Spence’s model, so it must come from the alignment of interests instead.

Babbling always exists: An uninformative equilibrium is available at every level of bias, so informative communication is never guaranteed.
Only partitions are informative: The sender can announce which interval contains the state, never the state itself, because any finer mapping would unravel through exaggeration.
Intervals widen up the type space: Each cell is \(4b\) wider than the one below it, so the receiver learns least about the highest states.
Informativeness falls with bias: The maximum number of credible messages \(N^{*}(b)\) declines as interests diverge, and at \(b \geq \tfrac{1}{4}\) only babbling survives.

Coarseness hurts both parties, which is why the finest available partition Pareto dominates. Sender and receiver disagree about the level of the action but agree that tracking the state more closely is better.


3.4.2.3 Moral hazard
Moral hazard arises after a contract is signed, when one party takes actions the other cannot observe or verify. Because pay can only be conditioned on what a court could confirm, contracts must be written on outcomes rather than on effort itself. That single restriction generates every result in the section.

Under bilateral risk neutrality there is no loss: The franchise contract makes the manager the full residual claimant and restores the first-best. Unobservability alone costs nothing.
Risk aversion creates the agency cost: Incentive compatibility forces income risk onto a manager who dislikes it, and the risk premium she demands is the cost of the problem.
Pay tracks evidence, not profit: Wages follow the likelihood ratio, so an outcome is rewarded insofar as it signals high effort. With two outcomes the two orderings coincide, and the required wage spread is \(\Delta g/(p_H - p_L)\): the noisier the signal, the larger the spread and the worse an instrument high-powered pay becomes.
The distortion reaches the effort level: Where the agency cost is large, the owner buys low effort even when high effort would be socially efficient.
Hidden types compound the problem: When the manager’s cost of effort is itself private, the menu collapses to a single contract, the low-cost type earns a rent of \(\Delta g\), and the threshold for using high-powered pay at all rises sharply.




3.4.3 Conclusion
This chapter has shown how game-theoretic reasoning applies to economic problems where private information, rather than pure strategic conflict, is the central friction. Working through the damaged goods model showed how a monopolist designs a menu of contracts to screen consumers it cannot identify, why the low type’s product is degraded rather than the high type’s, and why a firm may rationally spend real resources to make its own product worse.
We then examined what can be communicated when nothing is at stake in the message itself. The Crawford–Sobel model showed that costless words can carry information when interests are sufficiently aligned, that this information is necessarily coarse, and that communication collapses entirely once the sender’s bias becomes severe.
Finally, we turned to moral hazard, where the informational gap concerns actions rather than characteristics, and traced how the tension between insurance and incentives makes the first-best unattainable and gives rise to the agency cost — and how adding a hidden type on top of the hidden action transfers a rent to the manager who finds effort cheap, while leaving the other on a flat wage.
Across all three settings the same lesson recurs: information asymmetries do not merely redistribute surplus, they destroy it, and the institutions you observe in practice — product ranges, deductibles, performance pay, central bank independence, delegated authority — are best understood as responses to that loss. These frameworks underpin a great deal of applied work in industrial organisation, public finance, corporate governance and regulation, and you will find the same constraints recurring wherever one party acts or decides on behalf of another.

title: 3  Applications of Game Theory
text:
3.1.1 How Your Learning Is Structured
This chapter covers the following core areas:

Monopolistic screening and the design of contract menus under asymmetric information.
The damaged goods model: quality degradation as a screening device.
Informational rents, screening, pooling, and exclusion as competing monopoly strategies.
Moral hazard and the distinction between hidden actions and hidden types.
The owner–manager model of moral hazard under observable effort, risk neutrality, and risk aversion.
Moral hazard when the manager’s cost of effort is itself private information.
Applications in insurance, financial regulation, employment, and agricultural contracts.
Cheap talk and the credibility of costless communication.
The Crawford–Sobel model in cheap talk, covering sender bias, babbling, and partition equilibria.



3.1.2 Your Learning Outcomes
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

Explain how market structure shapes informational distortions, comparing competitive and monopolistic screening.
Derive the optimal menu of contracts in a two-type screening problem and interpret the resulting informational rent.
Compare screening, pooling, and exclusion, and evaluate the welfare consequences of product degradation.
Distinguish moral hazard from adverse selection and explain why unobservable effort creates a contracting problem.
Characterise optimal contracts under observable effort, risk neutrality, and risk aversion.
Evaluate the agency cost of moral hazard and identify when high-powered incentives are unlikely to be optimal.
Derive the optimal menu of incentive contracts when the agent’s cost of effort is private information, and identify who earns a rent and whose contract is distorted.
Apply the principal–agent framework to insurance, financial regulation, and employment settings.
Explain why costless messages can convey credible information in some strategic settings but not others.
Apply the Crawford–Sobel model to determine how sender bias limits the informativeness of communication.
Assess the welfare consequences of coarse communication and compare cheap talk with delegation.



Check Your Knowledge
Before diving in, let’s see what you already know. Don’t worry if you are unsure — these questions are here to get you thinking about the key ideas you will cover in this chapter.

Question 1. A monopolist cannot observe how much each consumer values quality. What is the purpose of offering a menu of different products at different prices?

To reduce production costs across the product range.
To induce consumers to reveal their private information through their choices.
To ensure every consumer receives the same level of surplus.
To eliminate competition from rival firms.


Try again. A menu is designed to reveal information, not to lower costs. In some cases the inferior product is more expensive to produce.


Well done. This is the essence of screening: consumers self-select into the contract designed for their type.


Try again. Under screening, different types typically receive very different levels of surplus.


Try again. The monopolist faces no rivals. The problem is informational, not competitive.



Question 2. What does an incentive compatibility constraint require in a screening problem?

Each type weakly prefers the contract designed for it over any other contract on the menu.
Each type earns non-negative utility from participating.
The principal earns zero profit on each contract.
All types receive the same allocation.


Well done. Incentive compatibility rules out mimicry, so each type truthfully self-selects.


Try again. That is the individual rationality, or participation, constraint.


Try again. That is a feature of competitive screening, not a general incentive compatibility requirement.


Try again. Incentive compatibility is what makes different allocations sustainable.



Question 3. What distinguishes moral hazard from adverse selection?

Moral hazard involves hidden characteristics; adverse selection involves hidden actions.
Moral hazard concerns hidden actions taken after a contract is signed; adverse selection concerns hidden characteristics that exist beforehand.
Moral hazard arises only in insurance markets.
Moral hazard requires both parties to be risk averse.


Try again. This has the two the wrong way round.


Well done. The distinction is one of timing: moral hazard is a post-contractual problem, adverse selection a pre-contractual one.


Try again. The term originated with insurance underwriters, but the problem appears wherever one party acts on behalf of another.


Try again. Moral hazard arises from unobservable actions. Risk preferences affect the cost of the problem, not its existence.



Question 4. An owner cannot observe how hard a manager works, but can observe the profit the project generates. Why does paying the manager a flat wage fail to induce high effort?

Because a flat wage is always below the manager’s outside option.
Because the manager’s pay does not depend on the outcome, so she bears the cost of effort without any reward for it.
Because the owner cannot afford to pay a flat wage.
Because profit is a perfect signal of effort.


Try again. A flat wage can be set high enough to satisfy participation. The problem lies elsewhere.


Well done. With pay insensitive to outcomes, the manager saves the disutility of effort by shirking and loses nothing.


Try again. Affordability is not the issue. The issue is that a flat wage provides no incentive.


Try again. If profit perfectly revealed effort, the owner could simply infer it and moral hazard would disappear.



Question 5. Cheap talk refers to communication that is costless, unverifiable, and non-binding. Why might a receiver still pay attention to such a message?

Because lying carries a legal penalty.
Because the sender’s and receiver’s interests may be sufficiently aligned.
Because the sender pays a cost to send a more precise message.
Because the receiver can verify the message after the fact.


Try again. Cheap talk assumes no penalty for misreporting. Credibility must come from somewhere else.


Well done. When preferences are close enough, the sender has little to gain from misleading the receiver, so messages can carry information.


Try again. That describes costly signalling, where credibility comes from the cost differential across types.


Try again. Cheap talk assumes messages cannot be verified.
